content.text: Students synthesize what myths and modern retellings reveal about danger, courage, transformation, and belonging.
Myths help cultures explain the world, and modern authors adapt those patterns in new settings for new audiences.

In Lesson 43, students will submit a polished portfolio piece and participate in the culminating seminar. This lesson sits in SRSD Stage 6: Independent Performance as students revise and polish their own essays for submission.

Students revise Part 1: the Comparative Explanatory Essay for clarity, cohesion, formal academic language, and conventions. Students also strengthen Part 2: the Myth Comparison Visual so it clearly supports the essay’s shared idea.

Part B: Revise and Polish Your Draft
Quick Write
Directions:

First, revise your conclusion so it synthesizes across myths instead of repeating your introduction. Then, use the revision checklist to make at least two additional changes: one for cohesion or formal style and one for conventions. Writing Check
What It Means
Ask Yourself
Clear Thesis Statement
Your thesis tells the reader the main idea of your essay and what you will explain.
Did I clearly explain the shared idea in one sentence?
Relevant Evidence
Evidence is facts, examples, or details from the text that support your thesis.
Does my evidence connect directly to the shared idea?
Explanation of Evidence
After using evidence, you explain what it shows and why it matters.
Did I explain how my evidence reveals the shared idea or cultural value?
Transitions Between Paragraphs
Transitions are words or phrases that connect ideas and help the essay flow.
Did I use words like for example, therefore, as a result, or another reason to connect ideas?
Formal Tone
Academic writing sounds clear, serious, and formal. It avoids slang or informal language.
Did I avoid informal language like

, or
lots
Analytical Conclusion

Did I restate my thesis and explain why my idea matters?

Did I capitalize names like
Zeus

myths, or
Manhattan

Did I check commas and periods so my sentence is easy to read?

Connection to Today's Learning
Say:
Today we will use a rubric, a revision checklist, and partner feedback to make our essays more precise, polished, and ready to submit.
Students will evaluate where their drafts are strong and where revision is still needed as they move from drafting to polishing.
This mini-lesson teaches students how to revise a weak conclusion into a clear, polished synthesis that explains what texts reveal, not just what happens.
Language Study
Display and read aloud:
Weak conclusion sentence:
Greek myths and the lightning thief both have heroes and monsters they are about courage and identity
Revised conclusion sentence:
Across Greek myths and
The Lightning Thief
, heroes face danger that tests their courage and identity, which shows that myths often explain what people value when the world feels uncertain.
Teach: Revising for Synthesis and Conventions
Say:

In this lesson, we revise conclusions so they explain a shared idea across texts and follow correct writing conventions. Strong conclusions do more than list details. They clearly name the texts, explain a pattern, and show what the texts reveal.
Ask:
What problems do you notice in the weak conclusion?
It is not capitalized correctly, it is a run-on sentence, and it mostly lists ideas instead of explaining them.
Ask:
How is capitalization improved in the revised sentence?
“Greek” and “
The Lightning Thief
” are capitalized correctly.
Ask:
How is punctuation improved in the revised sentence?
The sentence is no longer a run-on and uses commas to separate ideas clearly.
Ask:
What shared idea is explained in the revised sentence?
It explains that heroes face danger that tests their courage and identity.
Ask:
What does the phrase
which shows that
do?
It introduces what the texts reveal or mean.
Ask:
How does the revised sentence show synthesis instead of summary?
It explains a bigger idea about what myths show about people instead of just listing details.
To revise a strong conclusion, we:
fix capitalization, punctuation, and spelling
name both texts clearly
explain a shared pattern or idea
use
which shows that
to explain what the texts reveal
This helps our writing sound clear, correct, and analytical.
Connection to Today’s Learning
Say:
In this lesson, you practiced revising a conclusion so it is both correct and meaningful. Next, you will apply this structure as you discuss and finalize your own explanatory writing.
Support students in revising conclusions to move from summary to synthesis while correcting capitalization, punctuation, and spelling for clarity and precision.
Language Focus:
Synthesis language (“Across . . . ,” “which shows that . . .”)
Academic nouns (courage, identity, values)
Capitalization of titles and proper nouns
Punctuation in complex sentences
Before Language Study (preparation step—optional)
Students underline one place in their conclusion that lists a detail and circle one place that explains a bigger idea.
Model how a weak conclusion lists events while a strong conclusion explains what the texts reveal.
Prompt students to name the specific convention they are revising (capitalization, punctuation, spelling).
Guide students to use frames like “Across . . .” and “which shows that . . .” to move toward synthesis.
You said “It talks about courage”—we can say: “Across both texts, courage is tested through danger.”
You listed what happens—we can say: “Which shows that these stories explain what people value when they face danger or uncertainty.”
Across ___ and ___, ___.
___, which shows that ___.
This conclusion is stronger because it explains ___ instead of just listing ___.
I revised this sentence by fixing ___ and adding ___.
Invite students to explain what the texts reveal in everyday language or a shared home language and then restate it in formal academic English.
Encourage students to build on comparison language they already use and refine it into precise academic phrasing.
If students focus only on conventions → Prompt: “What does your sentence reveal about the texts?”
If students only summarize → Prompt: “Finish this: ‘Together, these texts show that ___.’”
If students write run-on sentences → Prompt: “Where can you separate or combine ideas so the sentence is clear?”
Student identifies the difference between summary and synthesis.
Student explains how a sentence shows what the texts reveal.
Student identifies and corrects at least one capitalization, punctuation, or spelling error.

Struggling with

Distinguishing Summary vs. Synthesis: Provide frames such as “In the story, ___ happens” vs. “Together, these texts show ___” and have students sort examples. Teacher Tip

Keep peer feedback anchored in the writing, not in the writer. Remind students to comment on clarity of reasoning, relevance of evidence, formal style, and respectful, specific naming of myths and cultures rather than on whether a myth is “true” or on a partner’s personal beliefs.
Part A: Peer Review for Clear Thinking (W.6.5) (15 minutes)
Rehearse and Refine
Pair students so each partner has an essay draft, visual, rubric, peer feedback form, and highlighter.
Teach: Using the Rubric to Give Useful Feedback
Say:

When I give feedback, I do not try to fix every small mistake on the page. I read once for the big idea, and then I use the rubric to decide which revision would help the writer most. I begin with a strength, name the exact part of the essay I am talking about, and then suggest one next step tied to thesis clarity, evidence, cohesion, conclusion, or formal style. Helpful feedback sounds like coaching because it points to a specific move the writer can make.
Say these Directions:
Exchange essays and visuals with your partner. Read the draft once all the way through, then read it again with the Performance Task rubric, the Performance Task Handout, and the
Peer Feedback
Form.. Leave one strength and one next step about the thesis, evidence, cohesion, conclusion, and Myth Comparison Visual.
Ask:
What is one strength of your partner’s explanation?

One strength of this explanation is that your thesis clearly compares Percy and Odysseus by showing that home becomes a test of courage. Your paragraph explains that Percy returns home to protect his mother, while Odysseus returns to reclaim his kingdom.
Ask:
What is one revision that would make your partner’s reasoning or evidence clearer?

Your paragraph about Odysseus could be clearer if you explain how the evidence connects to your claim. For example, when Athena removes the mist and Odysseus recognizes Ithaca, the text says “he kissed the fertile ground.” You could explain that this moment shows how deeply he values his homeland.
Ask:
How well does the Myth Comparison Visual support the essay’s main idea?

Your Venn diagram supports the essay because it places Percy and Odysseus side by side. The middle section shows shared ideas like courage and danger, while the outer sections explain how Percy protects his family and Odysseus is grateful to be home.
Ask:
What revisions will you make in your own writing after considering your partner’s feedback?
Responses will vary.
Support students in using respectful, specific academic language to give revision feedback tied to reasoning, evidence, cohesion, and formal style.
Language Focus:
Feedback stems
Evidence-based comments
Comparative language
Visual-analysis language
Before Rehearse and Refine (preparation step—optional):
Have students rehearse one oral sentence using the frame “One strength of this explanation is ___ because ___.”
Encourage students to refer to a specific sentence, paragraph, or visual feature when giving feedback instead of speaking generally.
Redirect students away from only surface-level editing by asking what the writer is trying to prove and where that proof becomes unclear.
You said “This part is confusing.” We can explain that more clearly by saying “This paragraph could be clearer if the explanation connects the evidence back to the thesis.”
You said “The picture helps.” We can be more supportive by saying “The visual supports the comparison because it highlights both myths side by side.”
One strength of this explanation is ___ because ___.
This idea could be clearer if you ___.
Your conclusion effectively shows ___, but you could also include ___.
Invite students to orally rehearse feedback with a partner before writing it on the form.
Affirm that constructive feedback can sound different across languages and communities; help students translate that care into school-based feedback stems.
If students give praise without evidence → Prompt: Point to the sentence or part of the visual that makes you say that.
If students focus only on conventions → Prompt: Before you mention punctuation, tell the writer one place where the reasoning is strong or unclear.
Student gives at least one specific strength tied to thesis, evidence, conclusion, or visual support.
Student offers a revision suggestion that addresses meaning or cohesion, not only conventions.

Struggling with: Giving Specific Feedback
Offer the frame “In the paragraph about ___, one strength is ___” so students anchor feedback to a text location in the essay.
Struggling with: Commenting on Visuals

Ready for extension

Ask students to identify the single highest-leverage revision move their partner should make first and explain why that move matters most. Invite students to suggest one way the partner could tighten formal style by replacing a vague verb with a more precise academic verb.
Ready for extension: If students need an alternative way to show understanding

Part B: Revise and Polish Your Draft (W.6.5, L.6.2) (15 minutes)
Quick Write
Students keep their partner’s feedback, the Performance Task rubric, and their own draft in front of them. Confer first with students whose conclusions still summarize instead of synthesize.
Display the following writing model if needed for support and guidance:
Across
The Lightning Thief
and
The Odyssey

, a recurring pattern emerges in which heroes must face danger before they can truly return home. Percy returns to New York with a stronger sense of identity, while Odysseus recognizes Ithaca only after the mist is lifted and he understands where he belongs. When Percy returns home, he decides to face the truth about his family and protect his mother, showing that bravery continues even after the quest is over. As Percy reflects on the dangers he has faced, he realizes that “the real world is where the monsters are,” suggesting that courage is still necessary in everyday life. Together, these stories suggest that home is not simply a place to reach; it is a test of courage, memory, and responsibility. Riordan’s modern retelling shows that this ancient myth pattern still helps readers think about belonging in the present.
Teach: Choosing High-Leverage Revisions
Say:

I look at the rubric and ask where my reader might get lost or where my ending feels unfinished. If my conclusion only repeats my thesis, I revise it so it synthesizes the evidence and names a larger idea across myths. After that, I make two more purposeful changes: one for cohesion or formal style and one for conventions. Revision works best when I choose a few strong moves instead of trying to change everything at once.

Struggling with: Writing Analytical Conclusions

Provide one of these frames to complete: “Across these myths, a recurring pattern emerges in which ___, which shows ___ and reflects ___.” or “Together, these stories suggest that ___, emphasizing ___ as a core human value.”
Struggling with: Editing Conventions While Revising
Have students reread one sentence at a time and check it in this order: capital letters, punctuation, spelling.
Ready for extension

Ask students to revise one body paragraph so its last sentence explicitly connects the paragraph back to the thesis. Invite students to strengthen their visual by adding a title, labels, or a caption that uses the same analytical language as the essay.

Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.
